# Data preparation

For this analysis, a download script was written in order to obtain latest crime incidence data, it also converts this file to Parquet format to optimize performance.

```{python}
#| eval: false

import polars as pl
import requests
from pathlib import Path

def download_incidence():
    # script folder
    SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    # script-based routes
    csv_path = SCRIPT_DIR / "data" / "raw_fgj_files.csv"
    parquet_path = SCRIPT_DIR / "data" / "fgj_files.parquet"
    # Create folder
    csv_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    url = "https://tinyurl.com/fgj-files"
    print("Downloading ...")
    res = requests.get(url)
    res.raise_for_status()
    
    with open(csv_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(res.content)
    
    # save as parquet
    df = pl.read_csv(csv_path, encoding="latin-1")
    df.write_parquet(parquet_path)
    print(f"✅ Processed file saved at: {parquet_path}")

    # remove csv file to keep parquet only
    csv_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    print("✅ Removed csv file")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance='simple' icon='false'}
**Manual download**

If you are a `bash` user, you can easily execute this command in your terminal.

```{bash}
curl -L 'https://tinyurl.com/fgj-files' -o fgj_files.csv
```
:::

## Reading the dataset

```{python}
#| label: tbl-incidence-dataset
#| tbl-cap: Incidence dataset preview. <br><br> You can see the table is in wide format, so we will transform it to long format for our analysis.

import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

data = (
    pl.scan_parquet('data/fgj_files.parquet')
        .with_columns(
            pl.col("fecha_hecho").str.extract(r"(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})").alias("fecha_hecho")
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.col('fecha_hecho').str.to_date().alias('fecha_hecho')
        )
        .filter(pl.col('fecha_hecho') >= datetime(2014,1,1))
        .collect()
)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance='simple' icon='false'}
**A Note on Dataset**

The dataset contains 2,098,743 records, but it has many null values in diverse fields, for example, there are 101,207 null rows without latitude or longitude. We are losing around 5% of records due to incomplete information.
:::

Next, we will create a subset for pedestrian robbery only.

```{python}
df = (
    data
        .select('fecha_hecho','delito','colonia_hecho','alcaldia_hecho','latitud','longitud')
        .filter(pl.col('delito').str.contains('ROBO A TRANSEUNTE'))
        .drop_nulls()
)
```

The following code let us preview the pedestrian robbery data subset we will use for our analysis.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cdmx-theft
#| tbl-cap: Robbery of Pedestrians Dataset. <br><br> This is a preview of the cleaned dataset we will use for our analysis.

headers = {'fecha_hecho': 'Fecha hecho', 'delito': 'Delito', 
  'latitud': 'Latitud', 'longitud': 'Longitud'}

(
  df
    .sample(5)
    .to_pandas()
    .style
    .format({'fecha_hecho':"{:%Y-%m-%d}"})
    .hide(axis=0)
    .format_index(headers.get, axis=1)
)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance='simple' icon='false'}
**A Note on the Pedestrain Data Subset**

The robbery data subset contains 150,286 rows, but it has 26 rows without a date and 1,855 rows without latitude or longitude. We finally obtain a clean subset with 148,407 rows. Reducing around 1.25% the reords with complete information.
:::


# Model preparation

We have selected robbery of pedestrians in Mexico City, because these crimes are highly dependent on urban "hotspots" (metro stations, specific intersections, or commercial corridors), making them perfect for spatial clustering.

We will apply K-Means clustering for Pedestrian Robbery since it helps us identify spatial "hotspots." 
For example, clustering by latitude/longitude can reveal that 3 clusters are concentrated around Bellas Artes, Insurgentes, and Polanco.

We will cluster crimes based on their coordinates to find high-incidence areas.

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import plotly.express as px

X = df.select(["latitud", "longitud"])

# K-Means modelling
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=4, random_state=365)
clusters = kmeans.fit_predict(X)

# add clusters back to a DataFrame
df = (
  df
    .with_columns(
      pl.Series(name="cluster", values=clusters).cast(pl.Utf8)
    )
)
```

```{python}
distortions = []
k_range = range(1, 11)

for k in k_range:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=365, n_init=10)
    model.fit(X)
    distortions.append(model.inertia_)
```

Chart

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5), dpi=100)
plt.plot(k_range,
    distortions,
    'o-',

    markersize=8)

# Estética editorial

plt.xlabel("Number of Clusters (k)", fontsize=10)
plt.ylabel("Inercia (WCSS)", fontsize=10)

plt.gca().spines['top'].set_visible(False)
plt.gca().spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Point

gdf_neighborhoods = gpd.read_file("neighborhoods.json")

geometry = [Point(xy) for xy in zip(df["longitud"], df["latitud"])]
gdf_incidence = gpd.GeoDataFrame(df.to_pandas(), geometry=geometry, crs="EPSG:4326")

# 4. Hacer el join espacial: ¿En qué colonia cae cada punto?
gdf_end = gpd.sjoin(gdf_incidence, gdf_neighborhoods, how="left", predicate="within")

# 5. Volver a Polars para seguir con tu flujo "Everything as Code"
df_neighborhoods = pl.from_pandas(gdf_end.drop(columns="geometry"))
df_neighborhoods.head()
```

## Spatial Analysis

Identification of high-concentration zones (hotspots).

```{python}
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter_map(
    df_neighborhoods.to_pandas(),
    lat="latitud",
    lon="longitud",
    color="cluster",        # El resultado de tu K-Means
    hover_name="colonia_hecho",
    hover_data={
        "latitud": False,      # Ocultamos coordenadas en el tooltip
        "longitud": False,
        "delito": True,
        "fecha_hecho": True,
        "alcaldia_hecho": True,
    },
    color_discrete_sequence=["#004761", "#E3120B", "#00a398", "#7BA2B3"],
    zoom=9.5,
    height=600
)

# Ajustes estéticos finales
fig.update_layout(
    margin={"r":0,"t":40,"l":0,"b":0},
    title_text="Hotspots of Pedestrian Robbery in Mexico City by Neighborhood",
    title_x=0.05,
    map_style="carto-positron" # Equivalente al antiguo mapbox_style
)

fig.show()
```


```{python}
# Ver qué cluster tiene más delitos en promedio o está en el centro
resumen_clusters = (
  df
    .group_by("cluster")
    .agg(
      pl.count("delito").alias("total_delitos"),
      pl.col("latitud").mean().alias("centro_lat"),
      pl.col("longitud").mean().alias("centro_lon")
    )
    .sort("total_delitos", descending=True)
)
resumen_clusters
```

```{python}
import folium
import polars as pl

# 1. Definir tu paleta "The Economist" para consistencia
color_map = {
    0: "#004761", # Azul Oxford
    1: "#E3120B", # Rojo Seguridad
    2: "#00a398", # Verde Petróleo
    3: "#7BA2B3"  # Azul Acero
}

# 2. Inicializar el mapa en CDMX
m_resumen = folium.Map(
    location=[19.4326, -99.1332], 
    zoom_start=11, 
    tiles='cartodbpositron'
)

# 3. Iterar sobre los centroides calculados
# Convertimos el resumen a lista de diccionarios para el loop
for row in resumen_clusters.to_dicts():
    cluster_id = row["cluster"]
    color = color_map.get(cluster_id, "#333333")
    
    # El tamaño del círculo será proporcional al volumen de delitos
    # Usamos una raíz cuadrada o logaritmo para que no crezca desproporcionadamente
    radius_size = (row["total_delitos"] ** 0.5) / 5  

    # Crear el Popup con datos agregados
    popup_content = f"""
    <div style="font-family: 'Arial'; font-size: 13px; min-width: 150px;">
        <h4 style="margin:0; color:{color};">Cluster {cluster_id}</h4>
        <hr style="margin:5px 0;">
        <b>Total Delitos:</b> {row['total_delitos']:,}<br>
        <b>Lat:</b> {row['centro_lat']:.4f}<br>
        <b>Lon:</b> {row['centro_lon']:.4f}
    </div>
    """
    
    folium.CircleMarker(
        location=[row["centro_lat"], row["centro_lon"]],
        radius=radius_size,
        color=color,
        fill=True,
        fill_color=color,
        fill_opacity=0.6,
        popup=folium.Popup(popup_content, max_width=300)
    ).add_to(m_resumen)

# 4. Mostrar el mapa (Recuerda llamarlo al final para Quarto)
m_resumen
```
